newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed to decline Strasbourg invite, accept NATO.
newsitem.headline: Lebed to decline Strasbourg invite, accept NATO.

text.p: Russia's security chief Alexander Lebed said on Tuesday he would almost certainly spurn an invitation to speak about his Chechnya peace deal before the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg.

Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying aboard his plane heading for Chechnya that the Strasbourg trip was unlikely because the criminal code introduced by rebel leaders recently did not correspond to accepted human rights norms.
The code he mentioned is based on Islamic laws or Sharia. Lebed did not elaborate.

The assembly unleashed a political storm when members invited Lebed and the military head of the rebels, Aslan Maskhadov, to visit on September 23 and to take part in a hearing on the peace pact the two men signed on August 31.

The session was also expected to tackle the sensitive issue of human rights in Chechnya and Russia's top human rights activist, Sergei Kovalyov, told Interfax on Tuesday he might attend despite having had a heart operation earlier this month.
Kovalyov is fiercely opposed to Russia's heavy-handed dealing with Chechen separatism and blames Moscow's military for the loss of tens of thousands of civilian lives.

Official Moscow has gone out of its way to denounce the invitation to Maskhadov because it considers the war in Chechnya an internal affair and because no one has been invited from the Russian-installed Chechen government of Doku Zavgayev.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky has blasted the invitations as "rude interference in Russia's internal affairs".
"We deem it inappropriate to discuss this issue at an international forum," he told reporters last week.
Maskhadov said at the weekend he thought it was "important" to go to Strasbourg. But it was unclear that he would attend.
It was not immediately clear if an official Moscow delegation would come to Strasbourg because of the row.
Russia joined the Council of Europe, which aims to foster democracy and human rights, in February only after Moscow pledged to seek a peaceful settlement in Chechnya.
Leni Fischer, head of the Strasbourg Parliamentary Assembly of the 39-nation Council last Thursday rejected charges the council was interfering in Moscow's domestic policies.

"Human rights violations are never an internal affair," he said. "We invited the...two men who put an end to the fighting in Chechnya," Fischer said in a statement. He confirmed the invitation to Lebed and rebel chief-of- staff Aslan Maskhadov.
Maskhadov said in a television interview shown on Monday it would have been important for him to attend to tell the world "the truth" about the events in Chechnya.

Lebed, an ex-general and political outsider with big presidential ambitions, has been trying to expand his brief since June, when Yeltsin made him security adviser and secretary of the Security Council, an inner circle of top officials.
He told reporters on Tuesday he had accepted an invitation to visit NATO headquarters in Brussels on October 7 and 8 to discuss NATO enlargement and other issues.
Interfax quoted Lebed as saying that NATO's expansion plans "mean mistrust in Russia and its policy".

A separate Interfax report said Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov would take part, as expected, in an informal meeting with the counterparts from the Western military alliance in Norway at the end of this month.
